title: Does God Suffer?
subtitle: Classical impassibility, passibilism, and the qualified middle. Three accounts of whether God can be moved by our pain.
triageNote: That God is good, loving, and not the author of evil is first-order. Every view on this page affirms it. What divides faithful theologians is a question one layer down: whether the God who loves us suffers as we suffer, is genuinely affected by our pain, or loves us out of an unchanging fullness that is never diminished or overwhelmed. This is a real debate. It is fought between people who all kneel at the same cross and all confess that in Christ, God truly entered our suffering. It bears on immutability, on the cross, on how you pray in grief. Hold the love and goodness of God without flinching. Hold your theory of whether and how God suffers with care. The wisest believers have landed in different places. Each is guarding something the others can lose.
question: When your world falls apart, and you cry out to God, what is happening on his side. Does your pain reach him. Does he feel it. The Bible seems to say yes without hesitation: God is grieved, God is moved with compassion, God's heart recoils within him. And at the center of the faith stands a cross where God in Christ bleeds. And yet the church for most of its history confessed that God is impassible. He does not suffer, is not overcome by passions, is not made to ache by anything outside himself. That sounds, at first, like a contradiction or a cruelty. So the question is sharp and personal. Is the God you pray to in your worst hour a fellow sufferer who weeps with you, or an unmoved fullness whose love is steadier than any feeling. Or is the truth some careful third thing the tradition was reaching for all along. And what did the church mean by impassibility. It was never, in its best forms, the claim that God is cold. The dispute is not whether God loves. It is what kind of love a perfect, infinite, unchanging God has, and whether that love can be wounded.
whyItMatters:
This is not a seminar question. It is the question of the hospital waiting room. When a person you love is dying and you are pleading with God, what you believe about divine suffering is the difference between two very different prayers. If God suffers with you, you are not alone in the dark. The Lord is in the waiting room, weeping. If God is impassible, your comfort is of another kind. His love for you is not a mood that might pass, not a feeling that could be exhausted. It is an unchanging fullness that nothing in the universe can diminish or distract. Both of these are meant as comfort. They are different comforts. People in real grief reach for different ones.

It also touches the cross, which is the center of everything. The New Testament dares to speak of the blood of God, of the Lord of glory crucified. Every Christian must say that in Jesus Christ, God truly entered human suffering and died a human death. The question is how. Did the divine nature itself suffer, so that we can say God as God experienced the agony of Calvary. Or did the eternal Son suffer in the humanity he had taken. Really suffering as a man, while remaining, in his deity, the unchanging God who upholds the universe even from the cross. How you answer decides what you mean when you say God understands your pain.

And it shapes whether you can trust God's love at all. A love that can be wounded is a love you can recognize. It is the love you know from the people who have ached over you. But a love that can be wounded is also a love that can be overwhelmed, depleted, held hostage by the one who wounds it. A love that cannot be wounded sounds colder. But it is also unconquerable: it does not depend on your loveliness, does not run out, cannot be defeated by your darkness. The whole weight of the question is whether the deepest comfort is a God who feels your pain. Or a God whose love for you no pain can ever touch. The tradition has fought over this because both are precious. Losing either one costs you something you need.

positions.name: Classical impassibility
positions.inOneLine: God does not suffer, is not overcome by passions, and is never diminished or controlled by anything outside himself. This is not coldness but the perfection of a love that is pure, full, and unconquerable.
positions.bestCase:
Let me clear away the caricature first. Impassibility is almost always attacked in a form no serious theologian ever held. I do not say God is indifferent, unfeeling, a block of marble watching your tears without concern. I say something quite different and, I think, far more comforting. God's love and compassion are so perfect, so full, so entirely his own, that they are never wounded. Never depleted. Never held hostage by the one who suffers. Impassible does not mean apathetic. It means God's love is never a reaction forced on him from outside, never a passion in the old sense, a passio. Something done to you that you suffer and cannot control.

Think about what suffering actually is in a creature. To suffer is to be acted upon, to be changed by something outside you, to be diminished, to lose. My grief is a thing the world does to me against my will. It can grow until it crushes me. Now ask whether you want that in God. If God can be made to suffer by the evil in the world, then evil has power over God. The creature can wound the Creator. And the very God you are praying to for rescue is himself a victim, swept along in the flood you are drowning in. Thomas Weinandy puts the question exactly right: does God suffer. And his answer, which is the tradition's answer, is that God does not suffer because God is perfect love already, infinitely full. A love that is already infinite cannot be increased by your joy or decreased by your pain. That is not less than a suffering love. It is more. It is a love that has nothing to lose and therefore nothing it can be made to surrender. A love that meets you in the pit not as a fellow prisoner but as the one who is free and can lift you out.

What about the cross, the strongest objection. Here the tradition is precise and I will be too. In the incarnation, the eternal Son took to himself a full human nature, body and soul, with a human capacity to suffer. So the Son of God truly suffered, truly bled, truly died, in and according to that human nature he made his own. We can rightly say God the Son suffered. The one who suffered as man is a divine person. What we do not say is that the divine nature, as divine, was diminished, overwhelmed, or destroyed. For then the world ends. The same Son was upholding the universe by his word even as he hung there. The wonder of the cross is not that God ceased to be God to suffer. It is that God, without ceasing to be the unchanging fullness he is, made human suffering his own. Take that away and you do not get a more loving God. You get a God who needed the cross to complete himself, a God in process. And a God in process is a God who might not finish.

What about the grief of God in the Old Testament, the relenting, the compassion that recoils. Real, every word of it. But spoken in our language so we can bear it, the way a father stoops to a child. God reveals his settled, blazing opposition to sin and his tender commitment to his people in the only words we could understand. The words of human feeling. The reality those words point to is not less than human grief. It is the infinite, undiminishable love of which our grief is only a flickering shadow. So when you pray in the dark, you are not crying to a fellow victim. You are crying to the one love in the universe that cannot be put out.
advocates: much of the patristic and medieval tradition
modern retrievers such as Paul Gavrilyuk

positions.name: Passibilism: the suffering God
positions.inOneLine: The God revealed in the cross genuinely suffers and is truly affected by the pain of the world. A God who could not suffer could not love as the Bible says God loves, nor stand with us in the only way that finally comforts.
positions.bestCase:
I want to take you to the one place where, for me, the whole question is decided. A Roman cross, on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the Son of God is dying. The cross is not a footnote to the doctrine of God. It is the revelation of who God is. And what I see there is not an unmoved fullness untouched by the world's agony. I see God taking the worst the world can do into his own life. And I cannot, will not, say that the deity stood serenely back while only the humanity suffered. That carving of Christ in two, suffering in one nature and untouched in the other, protects God's tranquility at the cost of the gospel's heart. On the cross, God suffered. Jurgen Moltmann wrote The Crucified God out of the ashes of a century that made the old impassibility unbelievable. He says it plainly: the suffering of God is the ground of our hope, because a God who suffers is a God who is truly with us. Only the suffering God can help.

Consider what the impassible God asks me to believe about love. I am told that God loves me but cannot be moved by my pain. That my suffering reaches him only as something he eternally knew and was never affected by. But that is not what love is. Every love I have ever known that was worth the name was a love that could be wounded. A love that ached when the beloved ached, that was not safe from the beloved's pain. A love incapable of being hurt is incapable of the deepest love. When my child suffers, I suffer. If I did not, you would rightly question whether I loved at all. The tradition asks me to call God's unmoved serenity a higher love than a mother's grief over her dying child. I cannot do it. The Bible does not do it either. God's heart recoils within him; his compassion grows warm and tender; in all Israel's affliction he was afflicted. These are not stooping figures of speech to me. They are the truth about a God whose love is real enough to be wounded.

And consider the century I write in. After the camps, after the trenches, after the places where children were murdered in heaps. A God who watched from a serene and impassible eternity, untouched, is not a God I can worship or commend. The only God who can be believed in the presence of that horror is the God who was in the horror. Hanging on the gallows, suffering with the victims. A man in a death camp, watching a child slowly strangled on a rope, hears the question, where is God now. The only Christian answer is the one Moltmann gives: God is there, on the gallows. That is not weakness in God. It is the strength of a love that will go all the way down. A love that refuses to stay safe while its children burn. The impassible God is finally a God who keeps himself at a distance from the worst of our suffering. The God of the cross does not.
advocates: much of twentieth-century theology after the world wars
Kazoh Kitamori (Theology of the Pain of God)

positions.name: The qualified or mediating view
positions.inOneLine: God is impassible in the sense that he is never overwhelmed, depleted, or controlled by suffering. Yet he is not unmoved: he genuinely enters our suffering in Christ and freely wills to be affected by his people, sovereignly and without diminishment.
positions.bestCase:
I think both of my friends are guarding a treasure, and I do not want to lose either one. So let me try to hold them together. Not as a soggy compromise but as the more careful thing I believe the best of the tradition was always reaching for. The word impassible was doing two jobs. Once you separate them, much of the quarrel dissolves.

The first job, and the right one, was to deny that God is a victim. God is never overwhelmed by suffering, never depleted. His love is never exhausted, his purposes never derailed by the evil done to him or to his children. Suffering does not happen to God against his will, the way it happens to me. To this extent the classical tradition is simply correct, and I will not surrender it. A God who is the helpless co-victim of evil cannot save anyone from it. The passibilists, at their worst, give me a God who is in the flood with me but cannot get either of us out.

The second job, the one that overreached, was to deny that God is genuinely affected. That he feels, responds, grieves, enters in. Here I stand closer to my passibilist friend, but with a crucial difference. God is affected, but freely and sovereignly, not by compulsion from outside. Being a victim of passion is one thing, and the ancients rightly denied it of God. Freely willing to love in a way that grieves over sin and rejoices over repentance is another. Scripture asserts the second on nearly every page. God is not moved the way I am moved, dragged about by feelings I did not choose. But God is not unmoved. He has chosen, in sovereign freedom and out of his own fullness, to bind his heart to a people. And a heart bound to others will grieve when they wander. That grief is not weakness imposed on him. It is the freely willed cost of a love freely given.

And the cross is where this comes to its sharpest point. I say with the whole church that the eternal Son truly suffered, really, in the human nature he made his own. So we may truly say God suffered for us, the Lord of glory was crucified. But I refuse to say the divine nature was diminished or that God ceased upholding the world. That unmakes the universe and the gospel with it. So I land where I think Scripture lands. God is impassible in that nothing can defeat or deplete his love. And God is not impassible in the sense his critics fear, because he genuinely entered our suffering and genuinely grieves over us. The deepest comfort is not either a fellow victim or an unmoved stone. It is a love that stoops all the way into your suffering and is, at the same time, strong enough to carry you out. It was never in danger of going under with you.
advocates: a strand running through Bavinck and Barth
Rob Lister (God Is Impassible and Impassioned)
readings of Cyril that stress the Son suffering in the flesh

biblicalEvidence.summary: I the Lord do not change. God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Two texts that deny change and the kind of wavering that marks creaturely feeling. The scriptural ground of immutability and impassibility together.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a strong passibilism that has God genuinely altered, depleted, or overcome by what creatures do. These texts deny that God changes as a man does.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical impassibility takes these as decisive: the God who does not change cannot be moved in the passive, creaturely way. The passibilist answers that Numbers 23:19 denies God lies and wavers like a fickle man, not that God has no genuine feeling. Constancy of character is compatible with real responsiveness. The mediating view reads them as ruling out God being a victim of passion while leaving room for God's freely willed grief.

biblicalEvidence.summary: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. Then: for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst. God's heart is convulsed with compassion. And in the same breath he grounds his mercy in not being a man.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a flat impassibility that allows God no real inner movement, since God's heart is said to recoil and his compassion to grow warm. And hard for a simple passibilism, since God's not being a man is what restrains his wrath.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Passibilism reads the recoiling heart as genuine divine emotion, love at war with judgment within God. Classical impassibility reads it as Scripture portraying in human terms God's settled, perfect mercy. God's not being a man is exactly what keeps his compassion from the instability of human feeling. The mediating view treasures both halves: real divine pathos, grounded precisely in God being more than a man and therefore never overwhelmed by it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. God is said to share in the affliction of his people, to be afflicted in their affliction.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a strong impassibility, since God is described as afflicted along with his suffering people, sharing their distress.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Passibilism reads this straightforwardly: God suffers with his people. The qualified view reads it as God's chosen solidarity, genuinely entering their affliction by his presence and ultimately in Christ, without being depleted by it. Classical impassibility notes the textual difficulty in the verse and reads the affliction as God's compassionate, saving involvement. It is expressed in the language of shared feeling for our sake.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, central to the cross question
biblicalEvidence.summary: Care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. Paul speaks of the blood of God, attributing the suffering and death of Christ to God himself. The most direct statement that God suffered.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that keeps God wholly distant from the suffering of the cross. The church was bought with God's own blood. And hard for a crude passibilism. It must still say how the deity that upholds all things suffered without being destroyed.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All views take this as central. Classical impassibility reads it through the communication of attributes. Because the Son is a divine person, what he suffered in his human nature can be predicated of God. So God truly suffered as man without the divine nature being diminished. Passibilism reads the blood of God as meaning the divine life itself entered death. The qualified view sits between: God truly suffered in the assumed humanity, really his own, without the deity going under.

biblicalEvidence.summary: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The cry of dereliction from the cross, the Son crying out in the experience of abandonment. The sharpest expression of suffering at the heart of the Trinity.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a strong impassibility, since the cry seems to express real anguish and even rupture within the life of God. The Son forsaken by the Father.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Passibilism reads this as the suffering of God reaching into the very relations of the Trinity. The Father giving up the Son, both bearing the pain. Classical impassibility reads the cry as the human voice of the Son, praying the opening line of Psalm 22, which ends in vindication. The incarnate Son truly experiences dereliction in his humanity while the Trinity is never sundered. The qualified view holds the cry as a real human anguish of the divine Son, taken into God, without dividing the Trinity against itself.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The cross question, read by all
biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus wept. At the tomb of Lazarus, deeply moved and troubled, Jesus weeps. The shortest verse in the Bible shows God incarnate weeping at human death and grief.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that makes God incapable of being moved by human sorrow, since here God in the flesh weeps over it.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Passibilism reads the tears as the visible truth that God is moved by our grief. That compassion reaches into the divine life. Classical impassibility reads them as the genuine human tears of the incarnate Son, real grief in his human nature. That is exactly what the incarnation was for. The divine nature remains the unchanging fullness. The qualified view takes the tears as God in Christ truly entering and sharing our sorrow. He freely chose to take a nature that could weep.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Every good gift is from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. God is the unchanging source of all good, with no shifting like the turning of shadows.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view in which God is genuinely altered or destabilized by what happens to him. There is no variation or shadow of turning in him.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Classical impassibility takes this as confirming that God's goodness and love are constant, never destabilized by the world's pain. The qualified view agrees God's character and love never waver. But constancy of being is compatible with freely willed responsiveness. Passibilism reads no variation as moral constancy, God's reliable goodness, rather than a denial that God is affected by his creatures.

weighing:
My judgment, offered tentatively, the way one ought to offer a judgment about how the infinite God feels.

I find myself on the qualified or mediating view. I want to be honest about how I arrived there. I refused to give up either of the things the two harder positions are guarding. From the classical side, I cannot let go of the conviction that God is never a victim. When I pray in the worst hours, I am not crying to a fellow prisoner who is as swept up in the flood as I am. I am crying to the one whose love cannot be drowned, depleted, or defeated. That is precisely why he can pull me out. A God who merely suffers along with me, and can do no more, is a companion in despair, not a savior from it. Weinandy is right that a love already infinite cannot be increased by my joy or decreased by my pain. That is comfort, not coldness.

But I cannot follow strict impassibility all the way. The place it loses me is the same place it has always been weakest: the sheer, relentless witness of Scripture to a God who is moved. The heart that recoils in Hosea, the affliction shared in Isaiah, the tears at the tomb, the blood of God in Acts. Call every one of these a stooping figure of speech, with no reality of divine feeling behind it. Then the Bible's most tender language about God tells me almost nothing true about his inner life. I cannot believe that. So I say, with the mediating writers, that God is affected, but freely and sovereignly. Out of his own fullness rather than by compulsion from outside. He grieves because he has bound his heart to a people. That binding was his own free act of love. The grief is real but never imposed, never a defeat.

And the cross holds it all together for me. I will say with the whole church that God suffered, that the Lord of glory was crucified. That the eternal Son truly bore the worst in the human nature he made his own. And I will not say the deity was extinguished or that God ceased upholding the world. Because then there is no resurrection and no rescue. The God of the cross stoops all the way into your suffering and is, in the same act, strong enough to carry you out. That, tentatively, is where I land. I hold it as my best reading, not as a wall against the brothers who land elsewhere.
charitableDisagreement:
Be slow to weaponize this one. All three views are trying to comfort the suffering, and each can name a real loss in the others. If you hold classical impassibility, do not accuse the passibilist of denying God's transcendence out of mere sentiment. The passibilist is guarding the cross and the credibility of God's love in a century of atrocities. That is a serious thing to guard. If you hold passibilism, do not call the impassible God a cold idol. The tradition that confessed impassibility did so to protect you from a God who could be overwhelmed by evil, a God who might lose. That protection is love, not philosophy. And if you hold the qualified view, as I do, do not imagine you have transcended the debate. You are leaning on both of them and owe both your gratitude.

The worst versions of each are not what the best defenders mean. Impassibility, rightly stated, is not apathy. It is unconquerable love. Passibilism, rightly stated, is not a finite struggling God but the conviction that God's love is real enough to be wounded. Hold the conversation at its best, not its caricature.

So, is it a hill to die on. The goodness and love of God, yes, first-order, defended with everything. A God who is not good cannot be trusted. A God who does not love is not the God of the gospel. But whether and exactly how that good and loving God suffers is a second-order question. The church has held it inside its worship for two thousand years, between people who all meet at the same cross. Confess the love without flinching. Argue the mechanics of divine feeling with the humility owed to a mystery. And keep your arm around the believer who finds comfort in a different answer than yours.

relatedDebates.note: Impassibility is one edge of the larger question of whether God changes. If God is unchanging in being and character, the question is whether he can still be genuinely moved or responsive. The attributes page maps the immutability debate. The suffering question is its sharpest and most personal case.

relatedDebates.topic: The communication of attributes in Christ
relatedDebates.note: How can we say God suffered if the divine nature cannot suffer? The classical answer runs through the communication of attributes. Because the Son is one divine person with two natures, what is true of him in his humanity can be said of God. How tightly the natures relate, and what can be predicated across them, is an old Christological question that this debate depends on.

If God is moved by prayer and repentance, does he ever alter his course in response? The texts of God relenting sit close to the suffering texts. Whether God's responsiveness reaches to genuinely changing his mind is taken up on the foreknowledge page. There the debate runs between classical theism, open theism, and Molinism.
